Fit a lag sequential analysis model

Source: R/lsa.R
lsa.Rd

lsa() fits a lag sequential analysis model to event sequences, wide sequence tables, transition-count matrices, long event logs, or sequence objects from other packages. Lag sequential analysis (Sackett, 1979; Bakeman & Gottman, 1997) tests whether, in a stream of coded events, one state follows another more or less often than chance predicts.

The transitions observed at a given lag are counted into a table of antecedent (from) by consequent (to) states; an expected table is derived under the hypothesis that the two are independent; and each cell is tested with an adjusted residual (Haberman, 1979), a standard normal deviate that is positive when the transition is over-represented and negative when it is avoided. The significant cells define a lag transition network, and the tablewise likelihood-ratio and Pearson tests show whether there is any sequential dependence at all. For every cell, lsa() estimates the observed and expected counts, the transition probability, the adjusted residual and its p-value, Yule's Q, kappa and lift. The engine selects the test: the classical analysis of Bakeman and Quera (1995) by default; a two-cell (2 x 2) test with odds ratios; Sackett's bidirectional test on the symmetrised table; or the parallel and non-parallel dominance tests of Sackett (1979) and Wampold (1984). Self-transitions or any other cells that cannot occur by construction are declared as structural zeros, and the expected table is then fitted by iterative proportional fitting (Christensen, 1997). With group, one model is fitted per group on a shared state set so the groups can be compared.

It returns an lsa object, or with group an lsa_group object holding one fit per group.

The fit is read with transitions(), nodes(), tests(), initial() and transition_probabilities(), and drawn with plot.lsa(). To fit several lags at once use lsa_lags(); to assess the transitions use bootstrap_lsa(), certainty_lsa() or permute_lsa(); to compare groups use compare_lsa(). The engine wrappers lsa_classical(), lsa_two_cell(), lsa_bidirectional(), lsa_parallel_dominance() and lsa_nonparallel_dominance() are lsa() with engine fixed and return the same object.

Usage

lsa(
  data,
  lag = 1,
  engine = "classical",
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  alpha = 0.05,
  loops = TRUE,
  structural_zeros = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  group = NULL,
  actor = NULL,
  action = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  order = NULL,
  session = NULL,
  time_threshold = 900,
  custom_format = NULL,
  is_unix_time = FALSE,
  unix_time_unit = "seconds",
  params = list(),
  ...
)

lsa_classical(data, ...)

lsa_two_cell(data, ...)

lsa_bidirectional(data, ...)

lsa_parallel_dominance(data, ...)

lsa_nonparallel_dominance(data, ...)

Arguments

data

Sequences in any form accepted by lsa_data(): a vector, a list of sequences, a wide table (one row per sequence), a square transition-count matrix, or a tna, group_tna, tna_seq_data, tna_data, nestimate_data, netobject or stslist object. With action, a long event log (one row per event). NA and empty strings are missing values, not a state; to model missingness as a state, recode it first.

lag

Integer lag (default 1). Positive lags pair each event with the one lag steps later, negative lags with the one |lag| steps earlier. A transition-count matrix supports lag = 1 only.

engine

Name of a registered engine (default "classical"); the built-in engines are listed by list_lsa_engines().

alternative

Alternative hypothesis for the residual and kappa p-values: "two.sided" (default), "greater" or "less".

alpha

Significance level that flags a transition as significant (default 0.05).

loops

Keep self-transitions in the model (default TRUE). FALSE declares every self-transition a structural zero.

structural_zeros

Optional K x K 0/1 matrix in which 0 marks a transition that cannot occur; default NULL (none). Combined with loops = FALSE, the diagonal is also forbidden. Supported by the classical engine.

labels

Optional character vector of state names. Default NULL takes them from the data (sorted values of character input).

group

Optional grouping: one value per sequence, or, with a long event log, the name of a column that is constant within each sequence. Default NULL (one model).

actor, action, time, order, session

Column names for a long event log (all default NULL). Supplying action (the state column) switches to long-format input. Rows are grouped into sequences by actor, session, or both, ordered by order or else by time.

time_threshold

Gap in seconds that starts a new sequence when time is given and session is not (default 900).

custom_format

Optional strptime() format for the time column (default NULL).

is_unix_time

Read the time column as a Unix epoch (default FALSE).

unix_time_unit

Unit of the epoch: "seconds" (default), "milliseconds" or "microseconds".

params

Named list of engine-specific parameters (default list()).

...

Engine-specific parameters, merged into params. For the engine wrappers, any argument of lsa() other than engine.

Value

An object of class c("lsa", "cograph_network"). Read it with transitions() (one row per from -> to pair: from, to, lag, count, expected, prob, prob_col, adj_res, p, yules_q, kappa, kappa_z, kappa_p, lift, sign, significant, plus any engine-specific columns), nodes() (one row per state), tests() (one row per tablewise test), initial() (one row per state), transition_probabilities() and summary() (see lsa-methods). The object also stores the per-cell quantities as K x K matrices, the canonical lsa_data() input and the parameters of the call, for the inference and plotting functions.

With group, an object of class c("lsa_group", "list"): one lsa fit per group level. The reading verbs return the same tables with a leading group column, and summary() returns one row per group.

Long-format input

A long event log is turned into sequences before the model is fitted: one sequence per actor, per session, or per actor-session pair, or a single sequence when neither is given. Events are ordered within a sequence by order, or else by time; when time is given without session, a gap longer than time_threshold seconds starts a new sequence. If the session identifier is already unique across actors, pass it as actor and leave session unset. Check the number of sequences reported by summary(fit) against the number expected.

Conditions

Errors carry the class lagdynamics_error and one of:

  • lagdynamics_bad_input: invalid data, labels, group, structural-zero matrix or long-format column.

  • lagdynamics_unknown_engine: engine is not registered.

  • lagdynamics_missing_package: the engine needs a package that is not installed.

  • lagdynamics_no_transitions: the data contain no transition at the requested lag.

  • lagdynamics_unsupported_option: the engine does not support structural zeros.

  • lagdynamics_ipf_infeasible: the structural zeros leave a state with observed transitions but no permitted cell.

  • lagdynamics_needs_events: group was given with a transition-count matrix, which cannot be split.

A warning of class lagdynamics_structural_zero_counts is raised when the data contain transitions in cells declared structural zeros: the row and column totals then include transitions the model declares impossible, and the tablewise test and residuals are not interpretable.

References

Bakeman, R., & Gottman, J. M. (1997). Observing interaction: An introduction to sequential analysis (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

Bakeman, R., & Quera, V. (1995). Analyzing interaction: Sequential analysis with SDIS and GSEQ. Cambridge University Press.

Christensen, R. (1997). Log-linear models and logistic regression (2nd ed.). Springer.

Haberman, S. J. (1979). Analysis of qualitative data: Volume 2, New developments. Academic Press.

Sackett, G. P. (1979). The lag sequential analysis of contingency and cyclicity in behavioral interaction research. In J. D. Osofsky (Ed.), Handbook of infant development (pp. 623-649). Wiley.

Wampold, B. E. (1984). Tests of dominance in sequential categorical data. Psychological Bulletin, 96(2), 424-429.

The formula-by-formula source map is installed with the package at system.file("REFERENCES.md", package = "lagdynamics").

See also

transitions(), nodes(), tests(), initial() to read the fit; lsa_lags() for several lags; bootstrap_lsa(), permute_lsa() and compare_lsa() for inference; plot.lsa(); list_lsa_engines() and register_lsa_engine() for engines; lsa_data() for the accepted input forms.

Examples

fit <- lsa(engagement)
fit
#> Lag Sequential Analysis  -  classical  (lag 1, directed)
#>   3 states | 1734 transitions | 1870 events | 136 sequences
#>   states: Active, Average, Disengaged
#>   independence: G² = 618.3, df = 4, p <2e-16
#> 
#>   Significant transitions (p < 0.05): 7 of 9
#>   strongest over-represented (of 3):
#>     Active -> Active          z =  +21.7  ***
#>     Disengaged -> Disengaged  z =  +15.4  ***

#>     Average    0.368  ███████████████████████
